utterances.speaker: JUDGE HUNT
utterances.text: Please call the case.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Case number IT-98-32-T, the Prosecutor versus Mitar Vasiljevic.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HUNT
utterances.text: Mr. Domazet.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOMAZET
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOMAZET
utterances.text: Examined by Mr. Domazet: [Continued]

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Vasiljevic, good morning.

utterances.speaker: RADOMIR VASILJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Good morning.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Let us resume where we broke off yesterday, and that was - let me remind you - when we were discussing the way in which records are kept of your patients at the health centre; do you remember that?

utterances.speaker: RADOMIR VASILJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I do.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOMAZET
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I should like to ask the usher to show the witness D26, the original, in other words. Could this document be shown to the witness, please.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Mr. Vasiljevic, will you please have a look at the book and tell us whether you recognise it, and tell us what kind of document it is.

utterances.speaker: RADOMIR VASILJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I do recognise this book. It is a protocol of patients, as we call it, and it is kept in the departments of our health centre in Visegrad, and we have already explained what kind of data is entered into this book of records.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Is that the book that you referred to, protocol covering a definite period into which the names of patients who were treated at the centre are entered?

utterances.speaker: RADOMIR VASILJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That is indeed the book that we discussed and I spoke about, but I must point out that, in the health centre, we have a number of these books, and I have brought some of them with me which have still not been shown to the Court. My motive was to show Their Honours that such books are still kept, as this is an old method of keeping records of patients, so it may be rather difficult to understand that this -- in this day and age, medicine is still practised in this way in some part of the world.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Mr. Vasiljevic, did you bring to The Hague this book that is before you as well?

utterances.speaker: RADOMIR VASILJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I did.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Before we continue discussing this book further, you just said that you have in your possession several such protocols. My question to you is whether there is any other book of records covering this same period of time or are you referring to protocols relative to other time periods?

utterances.speaker: RADOMIR VASILJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: You see the books I have brought with me mostly relate to the period of 1992, 1993. As for the other books, they are in the health centre and if Their Honours would need to consult them, they are at their disposal.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Yes, but Mr. Vasiljevic, I'm asking you whether those protocols relate to other time periods or to the same time period covered by this particular book?

utterances.speaker: RADOMIR VASILJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Other time periods. Other time periods.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HUNT
utterances.text: Mr. Domazet, I don't think you've elicited any idea of when this book, this book that the doctor has in front of him, the period to which it relates. Is it to the relevant period?

utterances.speaker: MR. DOMAZET
utterances.text: Yes. Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Vasiljevic, will you please tell us what period does the book in front of you cover? Which patients were entered in this book, for what period of time?

utterances.speaker: RADOMIR VASILJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: This book covers the period from the 20th of April, 1992 until the 4th of July, 1992.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HUNT
utterances.text: I think we've got to get to this a little bit more quickly. What patients does it relate to, the first aid patients or the ones that are admitted into hospital? Are you able to answer that, Doctor? What patients do they relate to?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I'm sorry, I didn't know that the question was addressed to me. This protocol contains information on all patients that pass through the health centre, the first aid, or emergency department, regardless of whether they were sent home after that to be treated at home or whether they were sent on to a hospital to be hospitalised.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HUNT
utterances.text: Does that mean that there is a repetition, to some extent, of the details in the book that we saw yesterday?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Sorry, I don't understand what you're asking me.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HUNT
utterances.text: The book that we had yesterday, we were told, were the first aid department patients. Now, you said this book relates to every patient that goes through the health centre, regardless of what happens to him. So that the people who were in the book yesterday, they should also be found in that book that you've now got in front of you. Is that what you're saying.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] If I understand you correctly, the people you are mentioning were entered in some other book. That probably means that they came to the health centre on another date, and not on a date that is covered by the dates indicated on the cover of this book. So their names should not appear in this book and in some other book, unless you're referring to some other kind of protocol because --

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Your Honour, if I may assist the Court --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HUNT
utterances.text: I give up. But Mr. Domazet, let's get on to what this book is about. Can you tell me what it is?

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: It's the same book, Your Honour. He has just been shown the exhibit --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HUNT
utterances.text: The same book. It's not yet an exhibit, by the way.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Yes, I thought, as the very last piece of business --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HUNT
utterances.text: What are we going back to it for? Why are we going back to that book? We have heard a lot about it. Why do we need to hear from the doctor more about that book?

utterances.speaker: MR. DOMAZET
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, I just wanted the witness to identify the book. He brought the book to The Hague. He is the current director of the health centre, and I wanted him to recognise it as a document covering the relevant period of time.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HUNT
utterances.text: I'm sorry, Mr. Domazet, but this is becoming ludicrous. We have got to move on. Now, he has identified it. Ask your next question, and let's leave the book to one side. There's something we'll have to deal with about that anyway. But let's get on with the case.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOMAZET
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Mr. Vasiljevic, will you please open the book and find the number 5.353.

utterances.speaker: RADOMIR VASILJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Could you please repeat the number.

utterances.speaker: RADOMIR VASILJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I've found the number.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Will you please tell me, in view of the book you have in front of you, what date this refers to, what is the name of the patient, and what information has been entered about the patient?

utterances.speaker: RADOMIR VASILJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Under number 5353, the name Mitar Vasiljevic was entered, born in 1954, a native of Visegrad, a member of the Territorial Defence. He came to the health centre because of a fracture. An x-ray was made. The doctor advised Trodon of 50 milligrams, and 50 percent glucose, 20 cubic millimetres was administered by the nurse. After, he was dispatched to the orthopedic ward of Uzice hospital.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you, Doctor. The only thing you didn't tell us was the date this entry was made. Can you see the date?

utterances.speaker: RADOMIR VASILJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I can, but I was making the pause, as you advised me to. The date is the 14th of June, 1992.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Will you please look further on, under the number 5.461.

utterances.speaker: RADOMIR VASILJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I found it.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Will you tell us what the date is when that entry was made, what person it refers to, and very briefly what it is about.

utterances.speaker: RADOMIR VASILJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The entry under number 5461 is for a person called Mitar Knezevic from Visegrad, a member of the Territorial Defence and it is ulno se laterum regionalis, it's an injury of his right lower arm, a cut of his right lower arm when the tendons were cut in that same area. He -- his injury was bandaged and he was sent on to the surgery ward in Titovo Uzice. The wound was dressed, and another patient was sent together with him in the same ambulance, and this is noted down here.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Who is this other patient, as you can see from the book?

utterances.speaker: RADOMIR VASILJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The other patient is Nebojsa Kovac, also from Visegrad, but his date of birth has not been noted down here.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Was that patient sent to the Uzice hospital as well?

utterances.speaker: RADOMIR VASILJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: He was sent together with Mitar Knezevic.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you. Will you please look at entry number 5488.

utterances.speaker: RADOMIR VASILJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Under this number 5488, we have the name Mitar Mosic, 5488, Mitar Mosic, a member of the Territorial Defence from Visegrad. His diagnosis is under code 724, he received a vial of novalgetol.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Will you please -- I made a mistake with the number. Will you look at 5484. 5484, please.

utterances.speaker: RADOMIR VASILJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: 5484. The name of Novo Rajak has been entered, a member of the Territorial Defence, and it was a shot wound of his lower left leg. He was also sent to Titovo Uzice.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And the one before him, please, 5483, is it again an injury and a case when a patient was sent to Uzice? Will you tell us who it was?

utterances.speaker: RADOMIR VASILJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: 5483, we have the name of Stanko Trifkovic, a member of the Territorial Defence. Again, he had -- he was wounded. He was wounded by firearms in his upper arm. Aminofilin [phoen] and dexazon [phoen] were administered and he was also sent to the hospital in Uzice.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Will you tell us the dates; were they sent to the hospital in Uzice on the same date and on what date?

utterances.speaker: RADOMIR VASILJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know which two you're referring to.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Novo Rajak and Trifkovic. They are together in this protocol.

utterances.speaker: RADOMIR VASILJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Novo Rajak and Stanko Trifkovic were sent to the hospital in Uzice on the same day, and that is the 18th of June, 1992.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you. Would you please tell us, in the book that you have before you, were the entries made in that book by one and the same person or by different persons? I'm talking about the whole book, not that particular page.

utterances.speaker: RADOMIR VASILJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The entries are mostly made by different persons, mostly different persons. It may happen that one entry may be made by one nurse or one doctor or several people. Usually, the doctor enters the diagnosis, where the rest is entered by a nurse, but this is not a hard and fast rule, and it is possible to deviate from it.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: So the question, my question is: Is it possible to see different handwritings for the same day? Could the entries have been made by several nurses or does it always have to be one and the same nurse?

utterances.speaker: RADOMIR VASILJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: It does not necessarily have to be the same nurse. In that period of time, several nurses were working. So for us, it was quite unimportant whether this nurse or another nurse or a doctor would enter this or that piece of information in the book.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Just one more question about that book. Apart from this book for this period - and I'm talking about the period from the 20th of April until the 4th of July - is there any other book of records when you admit patients to your health centre?

utterances.speaker: RADOMIR VASILJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: As far as this period is concerned, in the centre, we also had a department for occupational medicine, and they may have a protocol of their own, an occupational medicine protocol, but that book did not contain these patients that are registered in this book.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Mr. Vasiljevic, you brought this book with you. Is that the original book from 1992 in which the names of patients were entered?

utterances.speaker: RADOMIR VASILJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: This is the only book covering that period and it is absolutely original, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOMAZET
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Could the witness please be shown Exhibit D11.1. These are potential witnesses, and I am referring to a letter of the health centre sent by the health centre to attorney Tanaskovic. Could the witness look at it and identify it, if possible. Could the B/C/S original be shown to the witness, please, because this is a translation, as far as I can see. I apologise. This is the English translation.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: So I won't ask you to identify it. I will just ask you whether you remember, at the request of attorney Tanaskovic, that you did send him a report about Mitar Vasiljevic, or rather, telling him when and where he was treated at your institution.

utterances.speaker: RADOMIR VASILJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: At the request of the attorney Mr. Radomir Tanaskovic, in the course of the year 2000, we issued and wrote a letter addressed to Mr. Tanaskovic in which, on the basis of the protocol in our possession, we wrote down the dates and the injuries and the treatment given to Mitar Vasiljevic, including dressing of his wound, transportation, and so on. And I think we also listed the checkups that Mitar Vasiljevic came for. Tanaskovic asked us to cover a fixed period of time. He didn't ask us to cover the whole wartime period, and that is what we did. We sent the -- an identical letter to the office of the liaison officer of Republika Srpska at his request. And in a telephone conversation with the liaison officer, we agreed that I could provide him this information but, because of the reasons mentioned yesterday, I could not give him the protocol itself. And his opinion was that such a letter would be quite sufficient to establish the relevant facts. And he did not insist on us sending the protocol books to his office.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HUNT
utterances.text: It's not clear to me, Mr. Domazet, who the "he" is there. Was it the liaison officer of the Republika Srpska or was it Mr. Tanaskovic?

utterances.speaker: MR. DOMAZET
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, my understanding is that, in addition to a report being sent to Mr. Tanaskovic, a similar report was requested by the liaison officer of Republika Srpska. And I was just going to ask the witness to explain that.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: So am I right? In addition to Mr. Tanaskovic, similar information was requested from you by the liaison officer with The Hague Tribunal of Republika Srpska?

utterances.speaker: RADOMIR VASILJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, your understanding is correct. That is what I was saying. In addition to sending a letter to the attorney Mr. Tanaskovic, the liaison officer requested the same information and was given the same information.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HUNT
utterances.text: I'm still not clear. The doctor has said, We agreed that I could provide him this information but, because of the reasons mentioned yesterday, I could not give him the protocol itself, and his opinion was that such a letter would be quite sufficient to establish the relevant facts. Now, who is the "he"? Is it what is now said to be the liaison officer of the Tribunal? I'm not sure that can be accurate, but it might be the liaison officer of the Office of the Prosecutor. I want to know the "he" is with whom the agreement was reached.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOMAZET
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Can you explain that, Mr. Vasiljevic? I think you understood the question of His Honour Judge Hunt.

utterances.speaker: RADOMIR VASILJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I understood it, but I'm referring to the liaison officer of Republika Srpska with The Hague Tribunal. I'm almost certain that that is what it said on the memorandum of his letter. The title may not be a hundred percent right, but I'm sure that that is what he was, a liaison officer with The Hague Tribunal.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Do you happen to remember what you were asked to do, as the director of the health centre?

utterances.speaker: RADOMIR VASILJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, I've already said that I was asked for the protocols, and that after telephone conversation which I had with the liaison officer, we reached an agreement that it would be sufficient if we were to write a paper similar to this paper and send this letter with the facts relevant to the treatment of Mr. Vasiljevic, Mitar.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And did you, indeed, send the document of that kind to the liaison officer with The Hague Tribunal and Republika Srpska?

utterances.speaker: RADOMIR VASILJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, we did send that document to the officer.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you. Could you now explain why you didn't send the originals of the protocol, if that was what you were asked for?

utterances.speaker: RADOMIR VASILJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, we didn't send them, and they were the reasons that I brought up yesterday. I wasn't able to send them for the simple reason that we are duty-bound by law to safeguard these documents. And we have a realistic need for them, a practical need, because people come to us and often seek information from the protocols.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I'm not quite sure I understand. You mean you have to keep the documents and -- to ensure that they are not lost, or is the reason that you need the document for further reference?

utterances.speaker: RADOMIR VASILJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, both, both reasons. We don't want the document lost, and also the liaison officer explained that he did not know whether the protocols could be returned to me. And as I say, we need the protocols and these documents in the health service for further reference. People sometimes need information from those books.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Was that the reason why you didn't give the original protocols to Mr. Tanaskovic either, up until now?

utterances.speaker: RADOMIR VASILJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, they are the only two reasons why we were not able to hand the protocols over to Mr. Tanaskovic.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Mr. Vasiljevic, you have brought the original protocols with you. Now, in addition to this book, have you brought another protocol book?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HUNT
utterances.text: He has told us that he brought several to show us that it was -- the same system is still being used in this day and age. Do we really need to go into that? They're not for the same period, you've already established that.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOMAZET
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, Your Honour. For the period up until the 4th of July, 1992. But in the witness report, we can see that in July and August, a record was made of the examination given Mitar Vasiljevic in the health centre, and I think that that is relevant period because it is three medical examinations that were recorded. So I should like to ask the witness to find those recorded in the book. I will give him the pages in photocopy, the pages where that medical examination occurs and is recorded. I will also ask that the photocopies be tendered into evidence, admitted into evidence.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Would you please find the book which records the examination of the 29th of July, 1992.

utterances.speaker: RADOMIR VASILJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Under number 90, and the date is the 29th of July, 1992, we have Vasiljevic Mitar, that's what it says, member of the Territorial Defence. The diagnosis is a fractura cruris l. sinistra, which means a fracture of the left lower leg. The doctor accorded Mitar Vasiljevic sick leave and sent him to a medical examination with an orthopaedic specialist.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: That's what it says in the book in front of you. Now I should like to ask you to take a look at the photocopy of the pages from that book, whether it is the same thing, and then I should like to present D27 to be admitted into evidence. The previous page was photocopied because of the date and then, on the next photocopy page, you will find number 90 which we're talking about.

utterances.speaker: RADOMIR VASILJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I can note that the photocopy corresponds in all ways to the original.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HUNT
utterances.text: Now you are tendering the photocopy and not the original; is that right, Mr. Domazet?

utterances.speaker: MR. DOMAZET
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, I think that there are two relevant dates from that book, and yes -- but I would like to tender the original into evidence as well.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HUNT
utterances.text: Well, we better get the other entry from that book first.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOMAZET
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Mr. Vasiljevic, in that same book, do you have the 21st of August, 1992? Would you take a look at that date? If not --

utterances.speaker: RADOMIR VASILJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, it's in the same book. Yes, it is.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Would you then take a look at that date as well. Under number 520, the record says, "Mitar Vasiljevic, member of the Territorial Defence," and the diagnosis is psychosis etilismus and fracture of the cruris dextra and sent to Uzice. Could you explain the diagnosis that you read out in Latin, what does it mean, what was the diagnosis?

utterances.speaker: RADOMIR VASILJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Psychosis is a psychiatric diagnosis and it is a disorder of the consciousness. Etilismus means drunkenness or alcoholism as well, you can use that translation too. And fractura cruris dextris means fracture of the right lower leg.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I should like to ask you to look at the photocopy and the pages for that date, 2C, if it is a photocopy of the original, if it is true to the original.

utterances.speaker: RADOMIR VASILJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I haven't got that photocopy.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: It will be given to you in just a moment.

utterances.speaker: RADOMIR VASILJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: This photocopy is true to the original as well.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Microphone please, counsel.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOMAZET
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Would you take a look and see whether the date the 25th of August is in that book.

utterances.speaker: RADOMIR VASILJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The 25th of August is in this book.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Is Mr. Mitar Vasiljevic recorded on the 25th of August as well?

utterances.speaker: RADOMIR VASILJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. He is recorded under number 605, Vasiljevic, Mitar, and the diagnosis is psychoneurosis reactiva, and he was administered a moditendum depot [phoen] injection, one, and was also given a medicament axa, 50 milligrams, with recommendations that he take it three times one tablet a day.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Would you please take a photocopy of that page now, the page on which you find number 605, and would the usher please hand the witness the copy.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HUNT
utterances.text: Mr. Domazet, I don't want there to be some problem later with the suggestion that there's been a wrong translation, but in relation to the injury of the 21st of August, the doctor told us that it related to the fracture of the right lower leg.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOMAZET
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HUNT
utterances.text: It's recorded on the 14th of June as being the left leg, left lower leg.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOMAZET
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HUNT
utterances.text: Well, that's the way it's recorded; as long as there's no later dispute about the accuracy of the translation. That's all.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOMAZET
utterances.text: [Interpretation] The interpretation is correct. I noticed that, and I want...

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Your Honour, just to correct the transcript, I don't believe that it's recorded "lower left leg" on the 14th of June. The entry says nothing more than --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HUNT
utterances.text: Well, on the document that is not in evidence, that talks about the left lower leg.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HUNT
utterances.text: Yes. Which he said had been taken from the books.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOMAZET
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: First of all, let me ask you, Mr. Vasiljevic, whether you recognise the photocopy as being the photocopy of the 25th of August date Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts. you read out. Is it a true copy?

utterances.speaker: RADOMIR VASILJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, the copy corresponds to the original.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Would you now take a look at the 21st of August, 1992 date where you read out that, in addition to two diagnoses, one was a psychiatric one, and one was with respect to the leg, and you said -- read out that it was a control examination of the fracture of the right leg.

utterances.speaker: RADOMIR VASILJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's what it says here.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Do you happen to know who entered -- who made the entry? Who entered that information into the book?

utterances.speaker: RADOMIR VASILJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Judging by the handwriting and signature in the column where the "comment" column remarks, we can conclude that it was my colleague, Dr. Nebojsa Moljevic, who wrote in the facts.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Nebojsa Moljevic was one of the doctors who worked in your health centre at that time. Is that right?

utterances.speaker: RADOMIR VASILJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, he was.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And judging by the handwriting, you would say that it was his. Is that right? Is that right?

utterances.speaker: RADOMIR VASILJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I would say that it was his handwriting, Dr. Moljevic's.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Can you explain why it would say "right leg" if the basic fracture information previously speaks of the left leg?

utterances.speaker: RADOMIR VASILJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The only explanation for this case is that it was miswritten, that it was written in haste, and it was a slip.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOMAZET
utterances.text: [Interpretation] May I now propose, Your Honour, that this protocol with the photocopies be admitted into evidence as D27.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HUNT
utterances.text: Any objection, Mr. Groome?

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: No, Your Honour. We'll note, for the record, that I received the photocopies yesterday, and I have never seen the actual book. I will ask for an opportunity to examine it.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HUNT
utterances.text: We'll deal with that with that motion that you filed. Very well. Exhibit D27. The photocopies are only for our own use, if I understand. If the original goes in, then the original is the one that is the exhibit. Do you want the photostats separately marked in some way?

utterances.speaker: MR. DOMAZET
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HUNT
utterances.text: Well, I don't know why. I'm just trying to think why we need two copies of the same document as an exhibit. We have got a photostat copy of Exhibit 26, for example, the earlier book, which is not a separately marked exhibit; it's just for our own use. We are very grateful that you provide them because we can mark them, but they are not separate exhibits.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOMAZET
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, I understood that each piece of evidence and exhibit must be prepared in six copies, and so the protocol, which is D26, was photocopied in six copies, whether you will be using it for your own use or whether it will be attached to the book itself, which should be returned when it is no longer required, when the Tribunal no longer requires it, whereas the photocopies would probably remain as evidence in the records. So that is the only reason why I prepared the photocopies of that book and submitted them in six copies.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HUNT
utterances.text: You are required to provide copies for the use of the Judges and a spare copy plus one as the exhibit itself, quite often, and for the Prosecution. But bearing in mind that the doctor wants the book back, you are right. It may be best if we note one of the photocopies as a separate exhibit so that it can remain after the book is finally returned. But we will need one, then, that has not been marked for 26 as well. It may be there is a copy we can use. I'll just check with the Court deputy. I gather you've got an extra copy of Exhibit 26. If you can give that to us, it will be marked 26/1. And one of these copies you've handed out now will be Exhibit 27/1.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOMAZET
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Mr. Vasiljevic, do you happen to know whether Mitar Vasiljevic, on any other occasion afterwards, had an injury of any kind?

utterances.speaker: RADOMIR VASILJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, judging by the dates mentioned, Mitar Vasiljevic had a number of injuries.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Do you happen to have records of a fracture of a leg which occurred after the 1992 one that we discussed?

utterances.speaker: RADOMIR VASILJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I do. I have a protocol which encompasses that time period as well.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Could you take a look and see if, under the 6th of May, 1993, there is an entry for Mitar Vasiljevic as a patient of the health centre.

utterances.speaker: RADOMIR VASILJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Under number 3053, we have a record of Mitar Vasiljevic from Visegrad with the diagnosis refractura cruris l. sinistra, but it doesn't say here where Vasiljevic was sent to for treatment, but the only possible place he could have been a patient of this type at that time could have been the Uzice hospital. That was the only place he would have been referred to.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Could you translate the Latin diagnosis, the one you just read out, and tell us the date under which the entry was made?

utterances.speaker: RADOMIR VASILJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The date is the 6th of May, 1993, and the diagnosis refractura cruris l. sinistra means repeated fracture of the lower leg of the left leg -- of the lower left leg.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Vasiljevic. Now, I should like to ask you a question with respect to entries into the book you just read out. For many of the names in the book, it says that they were TO, Territorial Defence, or it said the name of the company; first, second, third or fourth company. Can you tell me something about that? How did this entry come to be included? Do you know on the basis of what the patients were classed as either TO or as belonging to one of the four companies? How were the patients that came to you recorded in that fashion?

utterances.speaker: RADOMIR VASILJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, this type of entry was the result of necessity of the command staff in the army so that they were able to know where their soldiers were at any particular moment. That is why they required us at the health centre to indicate, in addition to the name and surname, the affiliation. Sometimes it is a platoon, sometimes it is a company to which these people belonged, and for a time, the commanders of the units would come to the health centre if they needed any information, usually towards the end of the day, towards evening, and they would take note that their soldier under such and such a name was being -- was on sick leave for such and such a reason or was in hospital in some other place for treatment. They would be able to see this in the records. So it was at the request of the officers, commanding officers, that we kept records of this kind with entries of this kind denoting the company or detachment or platoon the individuals belonged to, and we also kept records on the basis of these statements of the patients. We asked them which unit they belonged to. We would say, "Which unit do you belong to?" he would give us an answer, and we would write in the entry for our records.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Does that mean, the last comment you made, that you didn't check whether, in fact, that soldier belonged to that particular company or some other? You didn't verify that fact.

utterances.speaker: RADOMIR VASILJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, we did not verify whether a person belonged to a particular unit or not.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And the entry "TO," does that also mean that a person belonged to one of those companies? In other words, could you just put the generic TO and sometimes the actual company?

utterances.speaker: RADOMIR VASILJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: These were members of the same army and the same brigade, and the companies are lower-level units within brigades, that is, within the TO, within the Territorial Defence.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: If I understand your answer correctly, if only TO is indicated without further details regarding the company, that would not be a mistake because it meant that the person belonged to the same army. If an indication is given of the number of the company, that is just a more detailed indication of the unit that the person belonged to within the TO; am I right?

utterances.speaker: RADOMIR VASILJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, you understand what I am saying well. You have put it well so I have nothing more to add.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I was asking you this because I noticed in these protocols, in the same column, sometimes membership of the TO is indicated, and sometimes a particular company, so I think you've cleared that point up now. A moment ago, you told us who you assumed it was that signed -- that entered -- made this entry. Am I right in saying that it was not noted down in the protocol which particular doctor examined a patient?

utterances.speaker: RADOMIR VASILJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Under the column "notes," or "remarks," the signature of the doctor should figure, but it is not something that is decisive. This is a small medical establishment. All the doctors and staff members know one another, and I am probably able to recognise the handwriting of all my colleagues so that no one ever insisted on the necessity of a signature figuring in the protocol, though, in my opinion, that would be desirable.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: As far as I can see, at least, in the protocol, nowhere do we find the time indicated, the hour; only the date. Was this customary in the periods before this period and for this period or was it applicable to this period only?

utterances.speaker: RADOMIR VASILJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I do not know that the exact time or hour of the examination was ever, in any period of time, entered in the protocol.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: One more question. You mentioned your colleague Nebojsa Moljevic as the physician who may have made these entries. In those days, that is, in 1992, do you recollect how many years of service Dr. Nebojsa Moljevic had, that is, what was his status?

utterances.speaker: RADOMIR VASILJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I can't tell you exactly how many years of service he had, but I do know that Dr. Moljevic, at the time, was a trainee, which means that after graduation from medical school and that period of time. It was under one year between the time he had graduated and the time that we are talking about. It was less than a year.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOMAZET
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Mr. Vasiljevic. I have no further questions for the examination-in-chief of this witness.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HUNT
utterances.text: Mr. Groome. Cross-examined by Mr. Groome:

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Dr. Vasiljevic, I would like to take you back to the time you spent with Mr. Vasiljevic in jail. Can you tell us what your precise diagnosis of him was after you examined him?

utterances.speaker: RADOMIR VASILJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I didn't note down the exact diagnosis anywhere. As this visit took place quite late, I had to go back to the emergency department after that, so that that diagnosis hasn't been entered anywhere. If I had entered the diagnosis, again, it would be a psychoneurosis reactiva, a reactive psychoneurosis, a condition following intoxication and exhaustion.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: What, if any, medical therapies did you apply to him at the jail?

utterances.speaker: RADOMIR VASILJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I know that we put him on a drip of 5 percent glucose solution, a sedative, and some vitamins. And I don't recall anything else, whether we treated him in any other way.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now, what was the purpose of putting him on -- you say, I think, a drip of 5 percent glucose? What was the purpose of that?

utterances.speaker: RADOMIR VASILJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I think that I already said that I was informed by Captain Kovacevic and also by Mitar himself that he was refusing to eat, that he hadn't been eating for two days. And I was also told that when he was brought to the jail, he was inebriated. And I assumed that the glucose level in his blood had dropped. And judging by his appearance, too, that was the condition I found him in. So I decided to administer 5 percent glucose solution.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And you said you gave him a sedative. What sedative did you give him?

utterances.speaker: RADOMIR VASILJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I can't be sure, but probably Diazepam. But I'm not sure of that.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now, we've heard some description of problems with his stomach, failure to eat. Did you give him any kind of medication to settle his stomach?

utterances.speaker: RADOMIR VASILJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, I didn't give him any medication for his stomach. Because I probably didn't have anything on me anyway. And also Kovacevic said that Mitar would be released from jail, so I assumed that the next day or the day after, he would come to the medical centre or that I would be called again if he had any serious stomach trouble.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did you suggest to him that he should come to the medical centre for some follow-up treatment by some people at the centre?

utterances.speaker: RADOMIR VASILJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't remember advising him to do that or not advising him to do that.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: If a person in his condition hadn't eaten for a number of days, would a single drip or intravenous bag of 5 percent glucose, would that be enough to reconstitute the person, or would they need additional drips?

utterances.speaker: RADOMIR VASILJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: It is absolutely insufficient. A single, one-time drip cannot resolve the condition that Vasiljevic was in, permanently. But if Vasiljevic started to eat from then on, then one should not expect further problems along the lines of a drop in glucose level or any other stomach problems.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did you remain in the jail until the full bag of intravenous fluid entered his system?

utterances.speaker: RADOMIR VASILJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I had to stay because, as we doctors say, we have to switch off the drip, that is, remove the needle, clean the spot where the needle was placed, and clean it with alcohol and put a bandaid over it.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now, you've told us that your diagnosis at that time was in part psychoneurosis reactiva. Can I ask you to tell us what are the symptoms of that condition and which symptoms you observed in Mr. Vasiljevic?

utterances.speaker: RADOMIR VASILJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: In addition to a change in his mental state, one could clearly see fatigue and exhaustion. I'm afraid I can't remember anything more as to exactly how it all looked.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You've mentioned, I believe, a change in the mental state or a change in his mental state. Can you be more precise about what it was about his mental state that you observed?

utterances.speaker: RADOMIR VASILJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Vasiljevic was visibly agitated. I remember that his hands were trembling, the fingers of his hands. He was disinterested, indifferent, he didn't feel like talking. I remember he only just managed to talk to me, which was something quite unusual for Mitar Vasiljevic. It was not like him at all.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: The symptoms that you observed inside the jail, were they consistent with somebody who was an alcoholic and had been deprived of access to alcohol for the previous day or so? Were they consistent with that?

utterances.speaker: RADOMIR VASILJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: It could be said that the symptoms were close to symptoms of abstinence, and one could say that you are right.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Are there any symptoms that you observed in the jail that were clearly not symptoms of somebody going through withdrawal from alcohol but indicated some more serious or greater problem, any additional symptoms?

utterances.speaker: RADOMIR VASILJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: It is necessary to point out that Mitar was extremely depressed. I told you a moment ago that it was very difficult for me to establish contact with him, which is not typical of an abstinence crisis, and one might say that he also had some other psychological problems. He would not talk about his problems, at least, not in that environment.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Would you say he had other psychological problems? I mean, granted now that you are in a gaol and -- I'm sorry, I withdraw that. There was a nurse with you when you saw Mr. Vasiljevic; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: RADOMIR VASILJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And were there other people present when you were treating him?

utterances.speaker: RADOMIR VASILJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: There were other people present, but we asked them, if possible, to move away until we finished what we had come to do.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: His failure to discuss problems with you in the presence of the nurse, in and of itself, does not indicate any psychological defect, does it?

utterances.speaker: RADOMIR VASILJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, that was not what I was trying to say. I wasn't saying that the nurse was an obstacle to him talking about his problems. He refused to talk at all. He didn't want to talk about his condition. I only just managed to draw from him an explanation as to why he was in prison.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You've mentioned that he had other psychological problems. What I'm trying to get to is: What are the concrete observations that you made at that time in the cell that leads you to describe that conclusion to us here today?

utterances.speaker: RADOMIR VASILJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I've already told you that Mitar Vasiljevic's behaviour was absolutely opposite to the kind of behaviour he had as I knew him before. He was much quieter, much more anxious, though I don't know the reasons that prompted this anxiety.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Other than this being quieter and being what you perceived as anxious, any other symptoms that you observed that led you to an assessment of his mental state? Anything else you want to add?

utterances.speaker: RADOMIR VASILJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: In view of the time distance, I'm finding it hard to recollect all these things, and it is very difficult to give you any additional details about that particular incident.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Can you describe briefly for us what, if any, specialised training you have in the diagnosis of psychiatric illnesses?

utterances.speaker: RADOMIR VASILJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, you see, the specialisation I have completed has very little to do with psychiatry, though it has some points in common. But in those days, I was a GP, I was not a specialist. And the terms of reference of a general practitioner is not the treatment of mental conditions, but he is expected to be able to recognise and identify such conditions, and to send the patient -- refer the patient for consultation with a neuropsychiatrist.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: So can you tell us what neuropsychiatrist you referred Mr. Vasiljevic to for your observations or diagnosis of him on this day?

utterances.speaker: RADOMIR VASILJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: On that day, or that evening, or that night, Vasiljevic was not referred anywhere, though I have already said that it was suggested that he come for an examination the next day, and then probably he would be referred on. As this was not an emergency, travelling at night, in those days, was unsafe and that was probably the reason for delaying referring Vasiljevic to additional examination. Such an examination could only have been done in Uzice.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: But what you seem clear about is you suggested to Mr. Vasiljevic that he come to the health centre after he was released from Uzamnica and to be further examined and for further action to be taken with regard to his condition; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: RADOMIR VASILJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now, at the time you spent with Mr. Vasiljevic, did he comply with your instructions when you needed to put in the IV and when you took other steps to examine him? Was he able to understand and comply with the instructions you gave him?

utterances.speaker: RADOMIR VASILJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, he was able to comply with such instructions, at least, that was my opinion.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now, Doctor, I'd like to ask you a few questions about this -- some of the medical books. Before I do, I would just maybe ask the Court, or ask Mr. Domazet through the Court, does he intend to tender the 1993 ledger? If not, I would seek to tender that so that I may examine it.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOMAZET
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, I had not intended to tender the 1993 protocol as this is not the period relevant for the indictment but I just asked for these entries because of other witnesses, but of course, I would not object if Mr. Groome should wish to tender this ledger.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HUNT
utterances.text: This document which is D11 does refer to an item in 1993, the 25th of February, 1993. It seems from the context in which it appears that it does relate to the injury with which we are dealing. The fact that it doesn't concern the relevant period of the indictment, if I may say so, doesn't deny the relevance of this material. Anyway, you want to see it in order to determine whether you want to tender it, I suppose, first, Mr. Groome.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Whatever mechanism is going to be most logical.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HUNT
utterances.text: But you want to look at it.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Yes, certainly.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HUNT
utterances.text: Well, in my view, you are entitled to look at it. How long do you think you'll be in cross-examination? I'm only trying to work out when we should deal with this motion of yours.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: I would think approximately an hour, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HUNT
utterances.text: Yes. We'll have to deal with this motion today. From the point of view of time, we've got to deal with it today. So at some stage we will, if necessary, have to stop the examination of the doctor in order to do so because I think it's a matter of considerable importance in the case. Very well. We'll adjourn now and resume again at 3.00.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HUNT
utterances.text: I'm afraid technical problems overcame us. Yes, Mr. Groome.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Your Honour, I spoke with Mr. Domazet during the break. And given that the Defence will seek the return of these exhibits, it seems that it may facilitate that future eventuality if it is tendered as a Defence exhibit rather than a Prosecution exhibit.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HUNT
utterances.text: I think so, but we can't force Mr. Domazet to tender it. They still get the return of documents of theirs which you have tendered.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: He has agreed to tender it as a Defence exhibit.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HUNT
utterances.text: All right. Okay. That will be Exhibit 28. What are the dates on it? I don't think we ever got them.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: It's a '93 ledger, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HUNT
utterances.text: Is that sufficient?

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: I believe it's May '93, but I'll rely on Mr. Domazet, if I'm incorrect.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HUNT
utterances.text: That will be Exhibit D28, the May 1993 protocol book. Yes, you proceed then, Mr. Groome.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Dr. Vasiljevic, I want to ask you a few specific questions about these records. First is there's an ordinal number that appears which appears in the first left-handed column of the records. Can you please describe for us how a particular patient is assigned that number?

utterances.speaker: RADOMIR VASILJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, the ordinal number is very simple. At the beginning of each protocol book, you have number 1. It starts off with number 1. And then it follows on, according to the order. Each patient get a number, 1, 2, 3, 4, and 578, for example, patient number 578. It's very simple. It goes by the patients coming to the health centre. When they come, they get a number following on from the order.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: So the numbers aren't continued from the book before, but every book begins afresh with the number 1. Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: RADOMIR VASILJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, that's correct.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Can I ask you to look at the first page in D26, and that's the book that covers the period April to July of 1992. I believe it's the brown one that's in front of you, the brown-covered one. If you would, would you tell us the first number in that book.

utterances.speaker: RADOMIR VASILJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The first number, 3.881.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: So is it still your testimony that each book begins with the number 1, or are the books consecutively numbered?

utterances.speaker: RADOMIR VASILJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, obviously in this case, it is consecutively numbered, following on from the previous document. Otherwise, you couldn't have such a high number at the beginning of this particular protocol book.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now, after this book, though, the other records you refer to -- I'm sorry, I don't recall the exhibit numbers, but the ledger or the protocol book from August of '92, that is renumbered. Correct?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HUNT
utterances.text: Exhibit 27. Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I ask you to take a look at Exhibit 27. It's the other book from the summer of '92.

utterances.speaker: RADOMIR VASILJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, that starts with number 1.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: So D26 from April to July continues the numbering system that was in place from the protocol book from before; but the book after D26, D27, the numbering is restarted. Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: RADOMIR VASILJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: In this particular protocol, the numbers start out from 1.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And that is in D27, the book from July and August of '92. Correct?

utterances.speaker: RADOMIR VASILJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now, I want you to go back to D26, the book from April to July, and I want you to look -- would you look up the date 20th of April. It's near the beginning of the book. If it helps you, the ordinal number will be 2833. Now, I would ask you, do you have the page that I'm asking you to look at, Doctor?

utterances.speaker: RADOMIR VASILJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The number you said is 2833.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Okay. I'm not asking you to look at that specific entry. I'm actually asking you to look at the entry, I think it's 2836 downward, and the question I have for you: Isn't it true that on this page the times are indicated on the protocol sheet. Isn't that correct? For example, 2846, there's a date 20/4/92 and then there's 1600.

utterances.speaker: RADOMIR VASILJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I apologise, but I seem to have the wrong protocol book.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: It's D26, it's the brown-cover one, I believe, sir. Not the yellow-cover one, the brown-colour one.

utterances.speaker: RADOMIR VASILJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Could you give me the number again, please?

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: 2836, it's the 20th of April. Doctor, again, I believe it's in the brown-covered book. I apologise, I might perhaps be reading the three as a two but it's the 20th of April, 1992. That's the day whose records I want you to take a look at now.

utterances.speaker: RADOMIR VASILJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I have found the 20th of April, 1992.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now, the time is indicated to the -- on the left-hand side of the protocols of the patients at the bottom of that page; correct?

utterances.speaker: RADOMIR VASILJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I have to agree with you that, looking here, I see that in some of them there is the time, but why that is so, I really cannot explain.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Doctor, I don't want you to review the thousands of protocol records at this stage, but would you agree with me that, in some cases, the time is recorded when patients arrive at the health centre? And I can point you to several other examples, if you wish, or will you agree with me that the time is indicated in some of the records in this protocol book?

utterances.speaker: RADOMIR VASILJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I agree with you.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now, Mr. Domazet asked you about Exhibit D11, which is a letter from you to Mr. Tanaskovic, and it was, I believe, your answering an inquiry by Mr. Tanaskovic regarding the times that Mr. Vasiljevic was treated in your hospital. Now, I believe you've testified that when fulfilling such inquiries about past treatments of patients, the only document that you rely on is the protocol book; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: RADOMIR VASILJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know whether I'd put it that way. The protocol book need not be the only source. The information that is sent at the request of courts, for example, or at the police or at the personal request of the patient can derive from a card, an index card of the patient, or patient card so that the protocol need not be the sole source of information.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I thought it was very clear now yesterday that the primary record, the only record that you have on a patient is this protocol book and that the card was given to the patient to carry around; is that not correct?

utterances.speaker: RADOMIR VASILJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't think you understood me, quite obviously. In view of our working hours, from 7.00 in the morning to 3.00 p.m., patients who come in after 3.00 p.m. cannot get his card because it is stored in the cards index of the health centre, which is closed after 3.00 p.m., so that patient doesn't have access to his card. If he comes for an examination between the hours of 7.00 in the morning and 3.00 in the afternoon, which are the working hours, the patient is able to access his card and then takes the card to the doctor examining him. But once again, let me stress that we're talking about normal times and not war. All patients and members of the army did not use cards at all regardless of whether they had them didn't have them. They didn't use them. Now, whether cards for a patient were opened or were not opened, no patient used a card as a means of record keeping.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Doctor, let me ask you, let's confine ourselves to the case of Mr. Vasiljevic. When you answered Mr. Tanaskovic's request for information regarding his treatment dates, did you regard other records aside from the protocol?

utterances.speaker: RADOMIR VASILJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, we used the protocol.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: So in fulfilling that request, you checked the different books that you now have in the courtroom here. That's how you fulfilled his request, by consulting the three different ledgers that you have in this courtroom now; correct?

utterances.speaker: RADOMIR VASILJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, correct.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now, I want to read you the first paragraph of the letter that you wrote to Mr. Tanaskovic. I believe that there is not a -- the original is not available in court, or so I'm informed. So I'll trust that the translation of what I read will refresh your memory. On the 14th of June, 1992, Mitar Vasiljevic came from medical examination of fracture left lower leg, diagnosis: Fractura cruris l. sin. The above-mentioned person was sent to general hospital in Uzice, orthopedic department. Now, Doctor, can you tell us which of the protocols did you rely on to write that paragraph in this letter?

utterances.speaker: RADOMIR VASILJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The protocol on the basis of which that paragraph was written has already been seen here and is known here. It is only part of the diagnosis that was introduced into the letter. Now, if I remember, in the letter, it only says "fracture," and it should have the complete diagnosis written out.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Can I have an agreement from Mr. Domazet that I am correctly reading the official translation of the original letter that we do not have here in court?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HUNT
utterances.text: I don't know if it's an official one. If it's an official one, they usually say so.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: I apologise; the translation that the Prosecution was provided, D11.

utterances.speaker: RADOMIR VASILJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The translation is probably correct. I don't have the B/C/S version in front of me at the moment, but I do believe that the translation is correct.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HUNT
utterances.text: Well, I think I can say that Mr. Groome certainly read the English version correctly, and it is the translation that you put forward of the original B/C/S.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Doctor, I would ask you to open up to the entry for Mr. Vasiljevic on the 14th of June. And again, that is ordinal number 5353. That would be in the brown ledger. After you read it, I would ask you to leave it open. I'll be asking you several questions about it. It's 5353 in the brown-covered book, 14th of June. You have Mr. Vasiljevic's entry in front of you now, Doctor?

utterances.speaker: RADOMIR VASILJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Does it say anywhere on -- in that entry, that it was a fracture of the lower left leg?

utterances.speaker: RADOMIR VASILJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, not in the protocol. The location of the fracture is not stated.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: In fact, Doctor, it doesn't even say "leg"; it simply says "fracture." So looking at that entry alone, it could have been a fracture of any bone in Mr. Vasiljevic's body. Correct?

utterances.speaker: RADOMIR VASILJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, you could draw that conclusion.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Before I ask you how you drew your conclusion, I want to ask you, we've referred now to three other entries from the medical protocol book in 1992. And if my memory serves me correct, there's only one reference to where the fracture occurred, and that was to the right leg, an incorrect reference. Do you agree with that?

utterances.speaker: RADOMIR VASILJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I agree that, in one place, it talks about the fracture of the right leg. As to the other facts, I don't remember them. I don't remember what it said, whether it said left or right.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Doctor, I'm going to have to ask you to review those records if you don't recollect. The first entry you refer to was on 729 of '92. I would ask you to leave the brown book open to the page you have it on. These other entries are all in the yellow book. And the ordinal number is 90.

utterances.speaker: RADOMIR VASILJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, under the ordinal number 90, it does say fractura cruris l. sinistra, which is a fracture of the lower left leg.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Doctor, how were you able to determine when you filled out Mr. Tanaskovic's request -- given conflicting information, one entry saying the right leg and one entry saying the left leg, how is it that you determined which was the correct statement of Mr. Vasiljevic's condition?

utterances.speaker: RADOMIR VASILJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: We have to clear up one point. Mr. Tanaskovic did not ask me to copy out the protocol. He asked me for information about treatment. So I could have written this out also on the basis of my own recollection, and on the basis of the statement of my colleague who was present at the time Mitar Vasiljevic was brought to the health centre and x-rayed and, after, transported to Uzice.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Who would that be?

utterances.speaker: RADOMIR VASILJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Mr. Loncarevic, Dr. Goran Loncarevic. He was present just then in the dispensary.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Is it your testimony now that you didn't fill out this request based on the protocols alone, but you spoke to the Dr. Loncarevic before drafting the letter to Mr. Tanaskovic? Is that what you're saying now?

utterances.speaker: RADOMIR VASILJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I cannot claim with certainty that I actually spoke to Mr. Loncarevic himself, but I must have spoken with someone to come to this conclusion which I wrote out and signed. As regards the protocol, as soon as I saw it, I noticed the shortcoming in the protocol. But there's nothing that can be done now. That is how it was written, and what happened happened.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now, Mr. Vasiljevic [sic] asked you about a request that you received through the liaison officer for the Republika Srpska regarding the Office of the Prosecutor's request to you to provide a copy of Mr. Vasiljevic's medical record from the 14th of June, 1992, and do you remember receiving that request?

utterances.speaker: RADOMIR VASILJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: We now know from what you've brought to us here in court that fulfilling that request would have required you to make a photocopy of a single page from that protocol; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: RADOMIR VASILJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, no. I was required to send all the protocols of the health centre -- maybe not all of them, but the protocols relating to a particular period in time. I was not asked to write a letter of this kind, but in a subsequent conversation with the gentleman, the liaison officer, we agreed that I could send him a similar letter to the one I had sent to Mr. Tanaskovic and that that would be sufficient, and that there was no need for me, in that case, to send him the protocols as well.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Well, we now have four photocopied pages before us. If you understood the request to be copies of medical records for a greater period of time, we are still talking about a very few documents, aren't we?

utterances.speaker: RADOMIR VASILJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: If I understood correctly the letter of the liaison officer - unfortunately, I do not have it on me - photocopies were out of the question. They were not admissible. In the first letter, the originals were requested, the original protocols.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Doctor, you did not answer the Prosecutor's request to send a copy of the medical entries that you've now shown us in court. That's correct, isn't it?

utterances.speaker: RADOMIR VASILJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I've already said that, in a telephone conversation with the liaison officer, it was agreed that it would be sufficient for me to write a letter of this kind to the liaison officer.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HUNT
utterances.text: Mr. Groome, it may be that the doctor's belief that there is a liaison officer who speaks on behalf of the Tribunal is wrong and that there is somebody from the OTP who writes with the name of the Tribunal on the top of it. But do you know anything about this liaison officer of whom the doctor speaks?

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: I know a request was made through a person designated in the Republika Srpska government to receive requests from the Office of the Prosecutor.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HUNT
utterances.text: And is it somebody within the RS government who is so designated or somebody from here who's been sent down there?

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Somebody from the RS government, Your Honour, that has been designated.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HUNT
utterances.text: I'm glad to hear that, that it wasn't somebody from the Tribunal. Anyway, let's assume that the doctor has this confusion. Was the request sent through this liaison officer?

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HUNT
utterances.text: That's where the problem arises, I think.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now, can you tell us, during this period of time, how long would a shift be for medical personnel? How long would a doctor be expected to work during this period of time?

utterances.speaker: RADOMIR VASILJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: We touched upon that matter yesterday, the question of working hours. Once the war broke out, all of us under the principles of work obligation were assigned to the work places that we held before or similar places within the health centre. But in view of the requirements of the job, as far as the emergency service was concerned, the wounded, and the injured, either civilians or military, the requirements were such that we had to be present as much as possible at the health centre. Say it was decided, you know, I use the word "self-organised," but I didn't mean that the health centre was self-organised. We just agreed amongst ourselves, in agreement with the director of the health centre at the time, and probably the municipal authorities or the military authorities, we arranged that we should be present at the health centre for 24 hours, round the clock. There was space provided for sleeping and for rest, and we took a rest when we had time. We took our meals at the health centre too. And roughly once a week, we would go home, and that is how we worked. However, in the administration of the health centre, the working hours were prescribed by the military authorities. I think it was from 7.00 or 8.00 a.m. until 4.00 p.m., something like that. I'm not quite sure. I know it was somewhat longer than the normal working hours before the war.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Doctor, let me see if I understand that a bit bitter. From what you've told us, it sounds that it was expected that doctors be on call 24 hours a day so that they were available close by in the hospital if they were needed; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: RADOMIR VASILJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, quite so.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now, having said that, am I correct in thinking that let's say one particular doctor would work a certain number of hours while another doctor was resting, and absent any emergency, that doctor would be allowed to rest and, at a particular time, he would be expected to come and relieve the first doctor? Am I correct in thinking that?

utterances.speaker: RADOMIR VASILJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: One could accept the way you put it. If there's work, we have to work, regardless of working hours. Sometimes there was just one of us working, sometimes both of us, because what would happen that you would have to deal with several wounded at the same time. On one occasion, there were 12 wounded men that were brought in in two ambulances at once. This wasn't so frequent that we had so many wounded people to deal with at once, but we worked in the way I just told you. We worked when necessary and we rested when the workload allowed us to rest. Whether it was in daytime or night-time, it depended on the influx of the sick and wounded.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Doctor, if I were on duty and there was no more than one patient coming in at a time, how many hours would I work before somebody would come and relieve me and take over from my duties?

utterances.speaker: RADOMIR VASILJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: You would work until you finish.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And what I'm trying to understand is -- what I'm trying to understand is you, as the director of the medical centre, what hours did you establish that I would work until I finished? Was it two shifts per day or three shifts per day?

utterances.speaker: RADOMIR VASILJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: First of all, let me tell you that, in those days, I was not the director of the health centre. And I repeat again: There were no fixed working hours. We were present at the health centre, which doesn't mean to say that we worked 24 hours a day, 360 [as interpreted] days a year. We were working when it was necessary. We were not when there was no patients. Whether we worked five hours or three hours or 13 hours, it was quite irrelevant.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Let me ask you this, Doctor: When you look in the medical records or the protocol, it seems that the handwriting filling in the protocol may be similar for six or ten entries, and then we see a different handwriting and that handwriting seems to follow for the next six or ten entries. What I'm trying to get at is would that indicate to us that there was a shift in personnel in the medical centre? Is that why there seems to be a difference in the handwriting on the same day of a protocol sheet?

utterances.speaker: RADOMIR VASILJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know what you mean when you say whether there was a change in shift. I'm repeating again, if the three of us were in the health centre, we wouldn't spend all our time in the area where we admitted patients and examined patients, in the emergency department. And it was quite irrelevant whether I would go down to the emergency service or my -- one of my colleagues or the other. Working hours did not play a part at that point in time. I don't know how to explain that to you. The fact that you see a change of handwriting, your theory could be accepted. Maybe one colleague took care of ten or so patients, and then another colleague would take over. Any such combinations were possible. But they don't change anything substantially.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Well, would you agree with me that the most probable explanation of a change in handwriting is that the person who wrote the first ten notes went and took some rest, and somebody came and began to see patients, and it was their handwriting that we see from that point forward? Would you agree with me that that is the most probable explanation of this shift in handwriting?

utterances.speaker: RADOMIR VASILJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: One could accept such an explanation, too.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now, going back to the day of the 14th of June, '92, I've counted 25 entries on that day. And please count them for yourself if you wish.

utterances.speaker: RADOMIR VASILJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: There's no need, if you have counted them.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now, Mr. Vasiljevic's entry is the third from the last. Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: RADOMIR VASILJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, that's correct. He's third from the front and third from the back.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You say third from the front. I know that there's a 14/6 on the top of the page; but if you flip back one page, there are more patients that were seen on the 14th. Correct?

utterances.speaker: RADOMIR VASILJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: So there were only two patients seen after Mr. Vasiljevic on that day. Correct?

utterances.speaker: RADOMIR VASILJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And what we can conclude from that is that either Mr. Vasiljevic was seen late in the day or in the night, or that it was very slow, there were very few patients seen during the night of the 14th. That would indicate one or the other. Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HUNT
utterances.text: I'm not clear why you say the night.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Late in the day, I should say.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HUNT
utterances.text: But will this not depend upon how many entries there are generally for each day?

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HUNT
utterances.text: Have you done an exercise on how many entries there are usually for each day?

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Obviously we can't, Your Honour. We're just confining ourselves to that day. Out of the 25 entries, it's the third from the last. And logic would tell us that either it was a very slow latter period -- if we were to divide entries, 25 entries by 24 hours, it would be approximately one per hour. It was either a very slow evening, or Mr. Vasiljevic was seen late in the day. Attempting to have the doctor agree to that proposition.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HUNT
utterances.text: Or it was an accident-free afternoon.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
